canonical_topic: Fair value accounting definitions: FASB ASC 820 and IASB IFRS 13
definition: In the U.S., the Financial Accounting Standards Board defines fair value under Accounting Standards Codification 820 (ASC 820); internationally, the International Accounting Standards Board defines it under International Financial Reporting Standards topic 13 (IFRS 13). Both define fair value as an exit price -- the price to liquidate a position under normal market conditions.
core_idea: The two major accounting regimes converge on defining mark-to-market's target value as an 'exit price,' the price obtainable to liquidate under typical market conditions, and both rank the reliability of that estimate via a fair value hierarchy.
key_points: FASB (US) defines fair value in ASC 820.
IASB (international) defines fair value in IFRS 13.
The two standards' definitions are similar in substance.
Fair value is defined as an exit price: the price to liquidate a transaction under typical/normal market conditions.
Both standards use a fair value hierarchy to communicate how accurate/reliable a given fair value estimate is.
relationships: Provides the accounting basis requiring firms to use mark-to-market
Related to primary market / highest-and-best-use valuation rules
caveats: Conflating 'fair value' with 'the price a firm believes an asset is worth' rather than the specific accounting definition of an achievable exit price.
